content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a new method of improving model performance on long-tailed datasets. 
It mainly consists of two modules. The first one is similarity window reweighting, which generates a set of weights for different classes. 
The second one is similarity window margin, which adjust the logits of a class. 
The combination of two modules leads to SWRM. 
They conduct the experiments on cifar-lt, imagenet-lt, and places-lt and the comparison of results validates the efficacy of proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
The consideration of a regional window seems novel. It only considers a limited classes each time and tends to be more focused. 

Cons:
1. the writing of this paper can be further improved for better understanding. 
2. The motivation of considering regional similarity can be improved to be more straightforward. 
3. The results in the experiments seem not good enough. For example, 
- The results on place-lt seems not good enough that only 36.36\% is achieved, which is worse than a variety of previous methods ( 37.9 
 in [1]).
 
4. The baselines considered in the experiments seem not enough. 
- The idea of using SWM to adjust logits is very similar to the operation in Logits Adjustment [2]. More comprehensive comparison across different datasets and backbones are needed. In this paper, they only compare the results on cifar. 

- The adopted baselines on places-lt are very limited. Only three paper before 2018 are considered. 

- The results on dataset inaturalist 2018 is also missing. 

5. (optional) Can the proposed methods be applied to transformer based models?

[1] Decoupling Representation and Classifier for Long-Tailed Recognition. Bingyi Kang, Saining Xie, Marcus Rohrbach, Zhicheng Yan, Albert Gordo, Jiashi Feng, Yannis Kalantidis

[2] Long-tail learning via logit adjustment. Aditya Krishna Menon, Sadeep Jayasumana, Ankit Singh Rawat, Himanshu Jain, Andreas Veit, Sanjiv Kumar
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The writing of this paper is not very clear and can be further improved.
1. The motivation of why introducing a regional window is weak. In the introduction, the tail samples are easily misclassified into head classes. To alleviate this phenomenon, a regional window is considered. The reason behind is not clear. 

2. In the end of section 3.2, the introduction of t-SNE seems confusing. 

3. Similarly, in section 3.3, the motivation of SWR is not clear. The design mechanism behind equation (2)  is also not clear.

4. From section 3.3 to 3.4, maybe an extra paragraph is needed to elaborate the connection between two parts. 

5. The design mechanism behind equation (2)  is also not clear. Can you give more illustration about this or add an illustration figure to elaborate this. 

6. The formulation of DySWRM seems missing, which makes it hard to understand. The differences between DySWRM are SWRM are also not very clear.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper considers regional similarity when computing weights for reweighting or marginal for rebalancing. This is good. However, the writing of this paper makes it hard to follow the details. Some analysis and baselines are also missing, which makes this paper less convincing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a sample reweighting algorithm SWRM for long-tailed recognition. Different from existing methods, the SWRM considers the sample number and feature similarity simultaneously to compute the weights of each sample. The experiments show its effectiveness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

--the proposed SWRM adopts a subtle designing for the sample reweighting which considers the confusion among visual features.

--The writing is clear and easy to follow.

--The motivation is straight. Sample reweighting considers the impact of feature similarity. 

Weaknesses:

--The novelty is simple and limited. The proposed method is still a revised sample reweighting, therefore, the representation space of tail classes is still low diversity. The improvement is limited.

--Some terms are confused, such as category similarity, category frequency difference..

--Comparison with SOTA long-tailed methods is missed, like PaCo, RIDE

--there are incorrect claim, such as  "The model trained on balanced datasets suffers catastrophic performance decline when evaluating it on long-tailed datasets."

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors study the problem of long-tailed visual recognition. The authors hypothesize that the representations learned by a deep network are suboptimal for the tail classes, which is the main source of the low performance for tail classes. Based on this, they propose measuring similarities between classes and using those similarities as weights and margins in loss functions. They report positive results on the common benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strenghts:
+ A novel approach for addressing class imbalance.
+ Strong results on several benchmarks.

Weaknesses:

1. The most important issue with the paper is that it is not providing sufficient explanations or motivations for several crucial design choices. For example: 

1.1. It is not clear why you require t-SNE distances to calculate similarity/distance between two feature points (average features). Why not simply calculate cosine/Euclidean distance?

1.2. Eq 2: More motivation and discussion should be provided for the form of this equation. E.g. why not multiply omit log and 1+? Why not take a form similar to effective number of samples calculation? 

1.3. The concept of the similarity window is not introduced sufficiently and the concept is left a bit ambiguous between Sections 3.2 and 3.3. As far as I understand, you sort the classes according to their similarities to class c, and if you have a window size W, you take only W closest classes in terms of similarity. This should be explained more clearly as "Upon projection vector, a sliding window is adopted to constrain the scope of similarity impact" is ambiguous.

2. The experimental evaluation is just looking at the cumulative performance scores (accuracy) and not analyzing the main claim in the Introduction, i.e., the claim that the tail-class representations are sub-optimal for especially distinguishing the visually similar tail and head classes. The authors should provide an analysis that their method is improving the learned representations.

3. Some other points that should be discussed or better phrased: 

3.1. Table 3 & 4: Is it not contradictory with your motivation that your approaches are not providing better performance for the few classes compared to the literature?

3.2. "We find that due to the easily confusable visual features residing in head- and tail classes, the model is apt to incorrectly classify tailed samples as head classes with similar visual appearance, as shown in Table 1" => You are taking the stance that lower performance for tail classes in an imbalanced setting is owing to a degrade in feature learning for the tail classes. This is against the commonly accepted hypothesis in the literature which proposes that the classifier training step is the main culprit. In the Introduction, this point should be discussed and made explicit.



Minor comments: 
- "most of them only focus on such a superficial phenomenon" => "superficial", though your reasoning may be correct, is a too strong word here. I would recommend justifying your reasoning more here and choosing a more politically correct word here.
- "Cifar100-LT" => "CIFAR100-LT". Similar problems in the rest of the paper.
- "PRELIMMINARY" => "PRELIMINARY".
- "model on to extract all image features" => Something is missing after "on".
- Eq 1: "log" => "\log" in Latex. Please also look up \left( and \right) parantheses in Latex. You can also benefit from the following guide on writing equations: http://www.ai.mit.edu/courses/6.899/papers/mermin.pdf
- "the all the average features." => "the average features."
- Eq 2: "*" => "\times" in Latex. 
- Table 2: Please write here whether these are errors or accuracies.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper generally proposes a more class-specific weight and margin calculation to enhance the performance of long-tailed recognition. The weight and margin are calculated as local similarity and sample number ratio instead of global distribution like previous methods do (i.e., weight and margin as functions of sample frequency in the whole dataset).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The intuition of utilizing local similarity to determine loss weights and margins is clearly explained. However, I don't think the idea of examing local confusion and similarity is new. For example, from OLTR, people already have discussed that tail classes are more likely to be miss-classified as head classes. Therefore, claims like "they do not analyze the long-tailed datasets and the model prediction results in depth" is wrong and condescending. Although the proposed method is intuitive, I think the novelty is relatively limited. The pipeline is first, to get a feature space from a plain cross-entropy loss, use t-SNE to project feature centroids to a 1-D space, and use the pair-wise distance in the 1-D space as class similarity. Based on this similarity and a predefined threshold (so-called sliding window size), they decide whether each class has confusing counterpart classes. If yes, weights/margins should be larger, and vice versa. To relieve the reliance on multi-stage training, they also proposes a single stage version (DySWRM), which does not require two stages of training. I think it is fine that the proposed method is simple, but what's missing is an ablation on whether use localized weights or not. SWR has a global reweighting component, n_max / n_c. It is important to see how much the local reweighting helped on top of this global reweighting to support the claims. In addition, if SWR has a global reweighting component, I don't see why SWM doesn't have it. 

On the other hand, although the proposed method has improved performance over reported baselines, a major line of works in long-tailed recognition (multi-experts), such as RIDE, ACE, TADE, is not discussed. It might be fine a few years back, but I think now, as all the state-of-the-art performance are from multi-expert models, it is necessary to at least have a discussion and consider the possibility of incorporating the proposed methods into one of the multi-expert models to see whether better performance can be achieved.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novelty is relatively limited. Code is not yet available. Clarity is ok, but the tone of this paper looks a little overconfident, making some claims too strong (e.g., the one example mentioned above).
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper might need some extra experiments and discussion.

content.title: SWRM: Similarity Window Reweighting and Margins for Long-Tailed Recognition
content.abstract: Real-world data usually obeys a long-tailed distribution. Many previous works merely focus on the superficial phenomenon that tail classes lack samples in long-tailed datasets, yet they do not conduct in-depth analysis on the datasets and the model prediction results. In this paper, we experimentally find that due to the easily confusing visual features between head- and tail classes, the cross-entropy model is prone to misclassify tailed samples as head classes with high appearance similarity. We propose a Similarity Window Reweighting and Margins (SWRM) algorithm to tackle this problem. Specifically, we pretrain a cross-entropy model to model category similarity, then a sliding window is adopted upon the modeling result to constrain the impact of similarity. We design weights for different classes with the help of similarity window, which is named Similarity Window Reweighting (SWR). Besides, different margins computed inside the similarity window will be assigned to different classes, this is called Similarity Window Margin (SWM). In a nutshell, SWR considers the category frequency difference and the category similarity impact simultaneously, so that the weight coefficients computed by SWR are more reasonable. SWM prompts the model to learn fine-grained features and is conducive to the model's discriminative ability. Therefore, our methods alleviate the issue of misclassification effectively. In order to enhance the robustness and generalization of the model, we introduce a learnable similarity vector and further propose a Dynamic Similarity Window Reweighting and Margins (DySWRM) algorithm, which spends less computation cost compared with SWRM. Extensive experiments verify our proposed approaches effectiveness and superiority over SOTA reweighting and logit adjustment methods.
